terms.gloss: the stock of a tree: the bottom of the trunk with its roots, and so what is left in the ground when the tree is cut or broken off
evidence: Verg. A. 12.208: scēptrum in silvīs īmō dē stirpe recīsum (Lewis & Short)
Cato Agr. 161.3: stirpēs fīent et intermorientur
terms.comment: Properly the lower part of the trunk together with the roots (Lewis & Short). Cato uses it of plants snapped off short, Livy of what sticks out of a rock face for a climber to hold. The other words name the trunk itself.

terms.gloss: the trunk or bole of a tree, without regard to its branches
the trunk or stock of a tree; a block of wood
a log, a post, a stake; a tree trunk

phrases.latin: nam sī dēfringēs, stirpēs fīent et intermorientur
phrases.english: for if you break them off, they will turn into stumps and die off

phrases.latin: manibusque retinēns virgulta ac stirpēs circā ēminentēs
phrases.english: and holding on with his hands to the bushes and stumps that stuck out round about

phrases.latin: quīn et caudicibus sectīs (mīrābile dictū) trūditur ē siccō rādīx oleāgina lignō
phrases.english: why, even when the trunk has been cut up (wonderful to tell) an olive root pushes out of the dry wood

sources: Lewis & Short: stirps · Lewis & Short: truncus · Lewis & Short: caudex · Lewis & Short: stipes
